title: Chapter 2: Conceptual Data Modeling: Entity-Relationship & Enhanced ER (EER)

sections.title: 1. Conceptual Foundations: Entities, Attributes & Keys
sections.description: Understanding the role of conceptual modeling in the DB lifecycle, attribute categorization, and key selection criteria.

blocks.title: The Database Design Lifecycle
blocks.content:
Designing a reliable database application is divided into two parallel lifecycles:

1. **Application Design (Software Engineering):** Requirements analysis $\to$ functional specification $\to$ transaction definition $\to$ application code implementation.
2. **Database Design (Data Architecture):** Focuses strictly on the organization, semantics, and integrity of data across three progressive abstraction phases:

```text
[Mini-World Requirements]
           │
           ▼
[1. Conceptual Modeling (MCD)] ──► Formalize real-world entities & business rules
           │                       (Entity-Relationship Model - independent of any DBMS!)
           ▼
[2. Logical Modeling (MLD)]    ──► Translate into relational table structures
           │                       (Relational Model: relations, foreign keys, 1NF/3NF)
           ▼
[3. Physical Modeling (MPD)]   ──► Optimize storage, partitioning & access paths
                                   (B+ Tree indexes, heap files, disk clusters)
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Conceptual Purity Rule:**
> The Entity-Relationship (ER) model is a **Conceptual Data Model (CDM / MCD)**. It must remain completely agnostic of technical implementation details such as SQL syntax, foreign key columns, table indexing, or vendor quirks.

blocks.title: Entities and Attribute Typology
blocks.content:
### Entities and Entity Types
* **Entity:** A distinct real-world thing or concept with an independent physical existence (e.g., a specific employee *John Smith*, a specific vehicle) or conceptual existence (e.g., a bank account, a university course).
* **Entity Type:** A collection (set) of entities that share the same attributes and structural definition (e.g., `EMPLOYEE`, `DEPARTMENT`).
* **Entity Set / Extension:** The collection of all entity instances belonging to an entity type currently stored in the database at time $t$.

### Complete Attribute Typology
Attributes describe the properties of entity types. In the ER model, attributes are categorized along four orthogonal dimensions:

1. **Simple (Atomic) vs Composite:**
   * *Simple:* Indivisible atomic values (e.g., `Salary`, `Gender`).
   * *Composite:* Can be divided into smaller sub-parts with independent meaning (e.g., `Address` subdivided into `StreetNumber`, `StreetName`, `City`, `PostalCode`). Useful when queries might target either the whole composite or individual components.
2. **Single-Valued vs Multi-Valued (`[0..*]` or `[1..*]`):**
   * *Single-Valued:* Holds at most one value for a given entity (e.g., `DateOfBirth`, `SSN`).
   * *Multi-Valued:* Can hold a set of values for a single entity (e.g., `Degrees[0..*]`, `PhoneNumbers[1..*]`). Indicated in UML/ER by bracket cardinality notation.
3. **Stored vs Derived:**
   * *Stored:* Raw values permanently preserved in storage (e.g., `BirthDate`).
   * *Derived (Calculated):* Values that can be dynamically computed from other stored attributes or related entities (e.g., `Age` computed from `current_date - BirthDate`, or `NumberOfEmployees` computed by counting related entities). Derived attributes are omitted from relational storage schemas to eliminate redundant drift.
4. **Mandatory vs Optional (NULL Semantics `[0..1]`):**
   * When an attribute may be unknown, missing, or inapplicable, it is marked optional as `[0..1]`.

blocks.title: Candidate Keys, Primary Keys & Natural vs Surrogate Selection
blocks.content:
### The Definition of a Key
An attribute or set of attributes $K$ is an **identifier (key)** of an entity type $E$ if and only if:
1. **Uniqueness:** No two distinct entity instances in any valid state have identical values for $K$ ($e_1[K] \neq e_2[K]$).
2. **Minimality:** No proper subset of $K$ satisfies the uniqueness condition. (A set of attributes satisfying uniqueness without minimality is a **Superkey**).

If an entity type has multiple minimal keys, each is called a **Candidate Key**. The database architect designates one candidate key as the **Primary Key (PK)**.

### The 3 Golden Rules of a Quality Primary Key
* **Absolute Uniqueness:** Must unequivocally distinguish every instance across all time.
* **Strict Immutability:** The key value must **never** need modification once assigned. Updating a primary key cascades through all referencing relations, risking deadlocks and orphaned records.
* **Compactness:** Should occupy minimal storage bytes (e.g., 4-byte or 8-byte integer) to maximize index memory density.

### Natural vs Artificial (Surrogate) Keys
* **Natural Key:** Formed by business attributes that already exist naturally in the mini-world (e.g., Social Security Number, vehicle VIN). *Risk:* Business rules change! If national regulations modify SSN formats or allow duplicates, database migrations become catastrophic.
* **Artificial / Surrogate Key:** An arbitrary, non-intelligent numeric identifier generated by the DBMS (e.g., `auto_increment`, `identity`, `UUID`, sequence). *Advantage:* Completely decoupled from business semantics, compact, and permanently immutable.

blocks.title: Superkey vs Candidate Key vs Primary Key
blocks.front: What is the formal mathematical hierarchy between a **Superkey**, a **Candidate Key**, and a **Primary Key**?
blocks.back:
* **Superkey:** Any attribute set $SK$ that guarantees uniqueness across all tuples in a relation ($t_1[SK] \neq t_2[SK]$). It may contain redundant extraneous attributes (e.g., `{SSN, LastName}`).
* **Candidate Key:** A **minimal** superkey. It guarantees uniqueness, but removing any single attribute destroys the uniqueness guarantee (e.g., `{SSN}`).
* **Primary Key:** The single designated candidate key chosen by the architect to uniquely identify entities and serve as the foreign key target across the database.
blocks.hint: Consider candidate keys as superkeys that have been pruned of all unnecessary attributes.

blocks.title: Natural Key vs Surrogate Key Trade-offs
blocks.front: What are the primary operational trade-offs between **Natural Keys** and **Surrogate Keys**?
blocks.back:
* **Natural Key:** Exists in the problem domain (e.g. IBAN, passport number). Convenient for human entry, but dangerous if real-world business specifications change, reassign numbers, or require format migrations.
* **Surrogate Key:** System-generated integer/UUID with no business meaning (e.g. `customer_id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`). Highly compact, completely immutable, guarantees optimal B-tree indexing, but requires human queries to join auxiliary tables to display meaningful names.
blocks.hint: Why does a banking system use an internal account_id integer even though customers know their account by IBAN?

sections.title: 2. Relationships, Roles & Cardinality Constraints
sections.description: Mastering binary relationships, recursive associations with role annotations, and the formal (min..max) vs UML cardinality notations.

blocks.title: Relationships, Degrees & Recursive Roles
blocks.content:
### Relationship Types and Relationship Instances
* **Relationship:** A meaningful association among two or more entity instances in the mini-world.
* **Relationship Type $R$:** A mathematical relation among $n$ entity types $E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n$, defining a set of associations: $R \subseteq E_1 \times E_2 \times \dots \times E_n$.
* **Degree of a Relationship:** The number of participating entity types. Degree 2 is **binary**; degree 3 is **ternary**; degree $n$ is **$n$-ary**.

### Recursive (Reflexive) Relationships & Role Annotations
When the same entity type participates more than once in a relationship type in different roles, it is a **recursive (reflexive) relationship**.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Mandatory Role Annotations:**
> In recursive relationships, role names **must** be explicitly written on the association ends. For example, in the recursive relationship `Supervision` on entity type `Employee`, one end must be labeled with the role `supervisor` and the other with `supervisee` (subordinate). Without role labels, the association is semantically ambiguous.

blocks.title: Recursive Supervision Relationship with Role Annotations
blocks.caption: An employee can be supervised by at most one supervisor (0..1), while a supervisor can oversee zero or more subordinates (0..*).

blocks.title: Cardinality Constraints: (min..max) Semantics vs UML Conventions
blocks.content:
Cardinality constraints specify structural restrictions on how entities participate in relationship instances.

### The $(min..max)$ Participation Notation
For an entity $e \in E$ participating in relationship $R$:
* $min$ specifies the **minimum** number of relationship instances $e$ must participate in ($min \ge 0$).
  * If $min = 0$: Participation is **partial (optional)**.
  * If $min \ge 1$: Participation is **total (mandatory)**.
* $max$ specifies the **maximum** number of relationship instances $e$ may participate in ($max \ge 1$, or $*$ for unbounded).
* Rule: $0 \le min \le max$.

### Notation Comparison: Min..Max vs UML Simplified Symbols

| UML Notation | Structural Meaning | Interpretation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `1..1` (or `1`) | Exactly one | Mandatory, unique relationship instance |
| `0..1` | Zero or one | Optional, at most one relationship instance |
| `1..*` | One or more | Mandatory, unbounded multiple relationship instances |
| `0..*` (or `*`) | Zero or more | Completely optional, unbounded multiple instances |
| `N` | Exactly $N$ | Fixed known count |
| `M..N` | Between $M$ and $N$ | Bounded window ($M \le N$) |

### Cardinality Ratios for Binary Relationships
Binary relationships are classified into four maximum ratio categories:
* **1:1 (One-to-One):** e.g., A department has at most 1 manager; an employee manages at most 1 department.
* **1:N (One-to-Many):** e.g., A department employs many employees; each employee works for exactly 1 department.
* **N:1 (Many-to-One):** The inverse of 1:N depending on viewing direction.
* **M:N (Many-to-Many):** e.g., An employee works on many projects; a project has many assigned employees.

blocks.title: Relationship Attributes (Attributes on Associations)
blocks.content:
Attributes can belong to relationship types rather than entity types when the value depends on the **combination** of the participating entities.

* **Example 1 (M:N):** The `hours_per_week` spent by an employee on a project cannot be placed in `EMPLOYEE` (an employee works varying hours across different projects), nor in `PROJECT` (a project has different hours for each assigned employee). It belongs strictly to the `Works_On` association.
* **Example 2 (1:N):** While relationship attributes on 1:N associations can technically be migrated to the $N$-side entity type (since each employee works for only one department, `start_date` of working there could sit on the employee), keeping it on the association preserves conceptual clarity.

blocks.title: Reading Cardinality Constraints in ER/UML
blocks.front: If the association `Works_For` between `Employee` and `Department` has `1..1` next to `Department` and `4..*` next to `Employee`, what does this mandate?
blocks.back:
* **Next to Department (`1..1`):** Every single Employee must work for *at least 1 and at most 1* Department (mandatory, exactly one employer).
* **Next to Employee (`4..*`):** Every Department must have *at least 4 and up to arbitrarily many (`*`)* Employees (a department cannot exist with fewer than 4 staff members).

In standard UML notation, the cardinality label at a connection end indicates the number of instances of THAT target class that can be linked to a single instance of the class at the opposite end.
blocks.hint: Read from the perspective of an individual instance of one side looking across the link to the other side.

sections.title: 3. Weak Entities, Higher-Degree Associations & Semantic Integrity
sections.description: Analyzing weak entity types with partial discriminators, higher-degree associations, and business integrity constraints.

blocks.title: Weak Entity Types & Partial Keys (Discriminators)
blocks.content:
### What is a Weak Entity Type?
A **Weak Entity Type (Entité Faible)** is an entity type that does not possess sufficient attributes to form its own primary key independently. Its identification and continued existence depend entirely on another entity type, termed the **Identifying Owner (Strong Entity)**.

### Core Properties of Weak Entities
1. **Existence Dependency:** A weak entity cannot exist in the database without being linked to an identifying owner entity instance. If the owner entity is deleted, the weak entity instances are typically deleted in cascade (`ON DELETE CASCADE`).
2. **Identifying Relationship:** The relationship linking the weak entity to its owner. In UML, this is depicted as a qualified association, where the partial key is placed in a qualifier box on the owner class.
3. **Partial Key (Discriminator):** A weak entity often has a partial key—an attribute that uniquely identifies weak entities *only within the context of a specific owner instance*.

$$\text{Primary Key of Weak Entity} = \text{Owner's Primary Key} \cup \text{Weak Entity's Partial Key}$$

* **Example:** In a corporate database, the `Dependent` entity has a partial key `first_name`. Two employees might both have a dependent named *Alice*, but within the scope of employee *SSN = 123-45-6789*, *Alice* is uniquely identified. The full key is `{SSN, first_name}`.

blocks.title: Weak Entity Modeling with Identifying Relationship
blocks.caption: DEPENDENT is a weak entity identified by the combination of its owner's SSN and its partial discriminator (dependent_name).

blocks.title: Higher-Degree ($n$-ary) Associations vs Binary Decomposition
blocks.content:
An association of degree 3 is **ternary**; degree $n$ is **$n$-ary** ($n > 2$). In UML, $n$-ary associations are explicitly drawn with a central association diamond connecting $n$ entity lines.

### Why $n$-ary Associations Are Not Equivalent to $n$ Binary Associations
A classic mistake in database design is naively decomposing a ternary association into three binary associations. Doing so introduces the **Connection Trap (Loss of Associative Semantics)**:

* Consider a hospital scenario: Doctors prescribe Treatments to Patients.
  * If modeled as three binary links (`Doctor-Treats-Patient`, `Doctor-Prescribes-Treatment`, `Patient-Receives-Treatment`), we know Doctor X treats Patient Y, Doctor X prescribes Chemotherapy, and Patient Y receives Chemotherapy. But we **cannot deduce** whether Doctor X actually prescribed Chemotherapy to Patient Y, or if Doctor Z did!
  * A true ternary association instance $\langle \text{Doctor X}, \text{Treatment C}, \text{Patient Y} \rangle$ binds the exact 3-way occurrence together atomically.

### Reading Cardinalities on $n$-ary Associations
To determine the cardinality constraint on one branch $E_1$ of an $n$-ary association, you must fix 1 instance of each of the other $(n-1)$ participating entity types together:
* *Question:* For a fixed specific pair $\langle \text{Doctor } d, \text{Patient } p \rangle$, how many `Treatments` can be administered? If at most 1, the cardinality on `Treatment` is `1` (or `0..1`). If arbitrarily many, it is `*`.

blocks.title: Semantic Integrity Constraints (Business Rules)
blocks.content:
Not all real-world business invariants can be captured visually through boxes, diamonds, and cardinality numbers on an ER diagram.

* **Definition:** A **Semantic Integrity Constraint** is a business rule governing data validity that exceeds the expressive power of standard ER constructs.
* **Examples:**
  * *"An employee's weekly planned hours across all assigned projects must not exceed 40 hours."*
  * *"A veterinarian can only conduct consultations in the specific clinic where they are permanently employed."*
  * *"A doctor who performs an operation must hold a medical specialty in Surgery."*
* **Methodology:** In conceptual modeling, these rules must be documented explicitly alongside the ER diagram as numbered **Semantic Constraints (CI)**. During logical and physical implementation, they are enforced through SQL `CHECK` constraints, stored procedures, or `TRIGGERS`.

blocks.title: Primary Key Construction for Weak Entities
blocks.front: How is the Primary Key of a weak entity constructed when mapped into relational structures?
blocks.back:
The Primary Key of a weak entity is always a **composite key** consisting of:
1. The Primary Key(s) of its identifying owner (strong) entity type(s), imported as foreign keys.
2. The partial discriminator key of the weak entity itself (if one exists).

If the weak entity has multiple identifying owners (e.g. an associative weak entity), the primary key combines the primary keys of all owners plus any local discriminator.
blocks.hint: A dependent's first name is only unique per parent employee.

sections.title: 4. Enhanced ER (EER): Specialization & Generalization Hierarchies
sections.description: Mastering the 4 canonical constraints on specialization: disjoint vs overlapping, total vs partial, and multiple inheritance lattices.

blocks.title: Specialization, Generalization & The Is-A Paradigm
blocks.content:
The **Enhanced Entity-Relationship (EER)** model extends classic ER with object-oriented conceptual modeling constructs:

* **Subclasses and Superclasses:** An entity type may have specialized subgroupings. For example, `Employee` is a superclass with subclasses `Secretary`, `Technician`, and `Engineer`.
* **The Is-A Relationship:** Every member of a subclass represents the *same real-world entity* as the superclass instance, but with a more specialized role. An entity cannot exist solely as a subclass member without also being an instance of the superclass.
* **Attribute & Association Inheritance:** An entity instance in a subclass automatically inherits:
  1. Every attribute of its superclass (including the primary key!).
  2. Every relationship participation of its superclass.
* **Local / Specific Attributes:** A subclass defines only its unique local attributes (e.g., `typing_speed` on `Secretary`, `certification_level` on `Technician`).

### Specialization vs Generalization
* **Specialization (Top-Down):** Starting with a general entity type and identifying meaningful sub-distinctions based on job roles, payment methods, or entity states.
* **Generalization (Bottom-Up):** Identifying common shared attributes across distinct entity types (`Car`, `Truck`, `Motorcycle`) and abstracting them into a unified superclass (`Vehicle`).

blocks.title: The 4 Canonical Specialization Constraints
blocks.content:
Specialization hierarchies are governed by two orthogonal structural constraints:

### 1. Disjointness Constraint: Disjoint vs Overlapping
* **Disjoint (`{disjoint}`):** An entity instance can be a member of **at most one** subclass in the specialization. Subclass sets are mutually exclusive ($\text{Sub}_1 \cap \text{Sub}_2 = \emptyset$).
* **Overlapping (`{overlapping}`):** An entity instance can simultaneously belong to **multiple** subclasses (e.g., an employee can be both an `Engineer` and a `Manager`).

### 2. Completeness Constraint: Total vs Partial
* **Total (`{total}`):** Every entity instance in the superclass **must** belong to at least one subclass in the specialization ($\bigcup \text{Sub}_i = \text{Super}$). No generic superclass instances can exist without a subclass role.
* **Partial (`{partial}`):** An entity instance may belong to the superclass without belonging to any of its subclasses (e.g., an employee who is neither an Engineer, Secretary, nor Technician).

### The $2 \times 2$ Specialization Matrix

| | **Disjoint (`{disjoint}`)** | **Overlapping (`{overlapping}`)** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Total (`{total}`)** | Every superclass instance belongs to **exactly one** subclass. | Every superclass instance belongs to **at least one** subclass (may belong to several). |
| **Partial (`{partial}`)** | A superclass instance belongs to **at most one** subclass (can belong to none). | A superclass instance can belong to **zero, one, or several** subclasses. |

blocks.title: EER Specialization Hierarchy with Constraint Annotations
blocks.caption: Employee specialization displaying both disjoint/partial work roles and disjoint/total payment methods.

blocks.title: Hierarchies vs Lattices (Multiple Inheritance)
blocks.content:
Specialization structures are classified by their inheritance topology:

* **Specialization Hierarchy (Tree):** Every subclass participates in only a single superclass-subclass relationship. Each subclass has exactly one direct parent superclass (single inheritance).
* **Specialization Lattice (DAG / Trellis):** A subclass can participate as a subclass in more than one superclass-subclass relationship. Such a class is called a **Shared Subclass (Sous-classe partagée)**.
  * *Example:* `EngineeringManager` inherits simultaneously from both `Engineer` and `Manager`, which in turn inherit from `Employee`. The shared subclass inherits the union of all attributes and associations from all its predecessor superclasses.

blocks.title: Synthesis: Evaluating Ternary Relationships vs Binary Decomposition
blocks.prompt: Suppose a veterinary clinic tracks that Veterinarians conduct Consultations for Animals, where each consultation takes place at a specific Clinic. Explain why creating three separate binary relationships (Vet-WorksAt-Clinic, Vet-Treats-Animal, Animal-RegisteredAt-Clinic) fails to preserve the exact facts of a consultation, and how a ternary association or associative entity resolves this.
self_check_criteria: Explained the Connection Trap: decomposing into three binary associations loses the atomic 3-way binding.
Demonstrated that binary links only show pairwise capability, not the specific combination instance.
Showed how a ternary association (or an associative entity `Consultation` with 3 foreign keys) captures the exact atomic event.
blocks.model_answer: Decomposing the 3-way relationship into three binary associations introduces a connection trap. With binary links, the database records that Vet V works at Clinic C, Vet V treats Animal A, and Animal A visited Clinic C. However, if Vet V works at multiple clinics, or Animal A was seen by multiple doctors at different clinics, the three binary tables cannot prove which specific clinic hosted Vet V's treatment of Animal A. A ternary association or an associative entity `Consultation` directly captures the 3-tuple <Vet, Animal, Clinic> as an indivisible atomic fact.

blocks.target_audience: a high school student learning programming
blocks.prompt: Explain what a weak entity and a partial key are using the analogy of hotel rooms inside different hotel buildings.
key_points_to_cover: Hotel room number (e.g. Room 204) is only unique inside that specific building (partial key / discriminator)
Room 204 cannot exist without the Hotel building (identifying owner / existence dependency)
To uniquely find a room worldwide, you need both the Hotel Name/ID + Room Number (composite primary key)

blocks.title: Interpreting UML Cardinalities on Binary Relationships
blocks.question: In a university database, the relationship `Advises` connects `Professor` and `GraduateStudent`. On the `GraduateStudent` side the cardinality is `0..5`, and on the `Professor` side the cardinality is `1..1`. What does this rule enforce?
options: Every graduate student must have exactly one professor advisor, and a professor can advise between 0 and 5 graduate students.
Every professor must advise exactly one student, and a student can have up to 5 professor advisors.
A graduate student can have no advisor or up to 5 advisors, and professors cannot have more than 1 student.
Professors and graduate students must be assigned in equal 1:1 pairs up to a maximum of 5.
blocks.correct_answer: Every graduate student must have exactly one professor advisor, and a professor can advise between 0 and 5 graduate students.
blocks.explanation: In standard UML reading, following from `GraduateStudent` toward `Professor` encounters `1..1`, meaning each student must have at least 1 and at most 1 advisor (mandatory, exactly one). Following from `Professor` toward `GraduateStudent` encounters `0..5`, meaning a professor may advise between 0 and 5 students.
hints: Look at the cardinality near Professor (`1..1`). Who is looking at the professor?
Look at the cardinality near GraduateStudent (`0..5`). How many students can one professor advise?

blocks.title: Classifying Specialization Constraints in EER Models
blocks.question: In a hospital database, every person registered must be either a Doctor, a Nurse, or a Patient. Furthermore, hospital security policy strictly forbids any person from occupying more than one of these three roles simultaneously. What classification describes this specialization?
blocks.explanation: Because every registered person must belong to one of the roles (no generic, unclassified persons exist), the specialization is Total. Because no person is permitted to hold more than one role at a time, the subclasses are mutually exclusive, which means the specialization is Disjoint. Hence, it is Disjoint and Total.
hints: Can a person exist in the database without being a Doctor, Nurse, or Patient? (Determines Total vs Partial)
Can a person be both a Doctor and a Patient at the same time? (Determines Disjoint vs Overlapping)

blocks.title: Identifying Primary Key of Weak Entities
blocks.question: A multinational firm has `Building` entities identified by `building_code`. Each building contains `Apartment` entities identified locally by `apt_number`. If `Apartment` is modeled as a weak entity of `Building`, what constitutes the primary key of `Apartment`?
options: An auto-generated surrogate key is strictly mandatory in the conceptual model
blocks.explanation: A weak entity is identified by the combination of its identifying owner's primary key (`building_code`) and its own partial discriminator key (`apt_number`). `apt_number` alone cannot identify an apartment globally because different buildings will have matching apartment numbers.
hints: Can two different buildings both have an 'Apartment 3B'?
How does a weak entity borrow identification from its owner?
